skill.name: Writing Hookify Rules
skill.description: Guidance skill for authoring hookify rules: markdown files with YAML frontmatter that define regex patterns and warning messages for Claude Code hook events (bash, file, stop, prompt). It explains rule syntax, condition fields, event types, and pattern-writing best practices.
skill.summary: Author hookify rules that watch for patterns and warn or block during Claude Code hook events.
skill.author: anthropics

security_audit.summary: This is a documentation-only skill (a single SKILL.md, 375 lines) that teaches how to author hookify guardrail rules. Every static finding resolves to a false positive: the flagged patterns (eval(, rm -rf, chmod 777, API_KEY=, .env, dd if=) appear as example regexes and prose inside documentation that teaches users to DETECT and WARN about these patterns — none is executable code, and the skill ships no scripts or network calls. No prompt injection, data-exfiltration intent, or business-logic abuse was found.

static_findings.snippet: Hookify rules are markdown files with YAML frontmatter that define patterns to watch for and message
- `block`: Prevent operation (PreToolUse) or stop session (Stop events)
- YAML quoted strings: `"pattern"` requires double backslashes `\\s`
You're adding an API key to a .env file. Ensure this file is in .gitignore!

remediation.issue: Static scanners repeatedly flag the example regex patterns (eval(, rm -rf, chmod 777, API_KEY=) as executable dangerous code.
remediation.suggestion: Consider fencing example patterns in clearly labeled code blocks or adding an inline note that these are illustrative detection patterns, not commands, to reduce false positives in downstream automated scanners.

content.user_title: Write Hookify Guardrail Rules for Claude Code
content.value_statement: Teams want consistent guardrails, but writing hookify rules by hand means guessing at YAML frontmatter, event types, and regex syntax. This skill gives Claude the exact rule format and pattern-writing guidance so it can author correct hookify rules that warn or block risky actions on the first try.
actual_capabilities: Explains the hookify rule file format: markdown with YAML frontmatter stored as .claude/hookify.{name}.local.md.
Documents every frontmatter field, including name, enabled, event, action, and pattern.
Covers all four event types (bash, file, stop, prompt) and the all wildcard, with an example for each.
Describes the advanced multi-condition format using field, operator, and pattern keys.
Provides regex writing guidance, including metacharacters, escaping, and common too-broad or too-specific pitfalls.
Recommends naming and file-organization conventions plus gitignore guidance for local rules.
limitations: It is documentation only. It teaches rule authoring and does not install, run, or enforce any rule itself.
It targets the hookify plugin format for Claude Code and does not cover other hook systems or CI linters.
It does not validate live patterns against a real codebase. The author must test rules after creating them.
It assumes Python-flavored regex, so patterns must follow that syntax rather than other regex dialects.

use_cases.title: Block destructive shell commands
use_cases.description: A developer wants Claude to stop before running commands like rm -rf. The skill helps write a bash-event rule that matches the pattern and blocks the operation.

use_cases.title: Warn about console.log in production code
use_cases.description: A team lead wants a gentle reminder when debug logging is added to source files. The skill helps write a file-event rule that warns without blocking.

use_cases.title: Enforce a pre-stop checklist
use_cases.description: A release manager wants a completion checklist shown before the agent stops. The skill helps write a stop-event rule that lists required steps like running tests and updating docs.

prompt_templates.title: Create a basic warning rule
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a hookify rule that warns me whenever I add console.log to a JavaScript or TypeScript file.

prompt_templates.title: Block a dangerous command
prompt_templates.prompt: Write a hookify rule that blocks any bash command matching rm -rf and explains why it was blocked.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: a bash-event rule with the block action.

prompt_templates.prompt: Create a hookify rule that triggers only when a .env file is edited and the change contains API_KEY, then reminds me to add the file to gitignore.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: a file-event rule using two conditions with different operators.

prompt_templates.title: Build a pre-stop checklist rule
prompt_templates.prompt: Write a hookify stop-event rule that shows a completion checklist covering tests, build status, and documentation before the agent finishes.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: a stop-event rule matching all sessions with a formatted checklist message.

output_examples.input: Create a hookify rule that warns me when I add console.log to a TypeScript file.
output_examples.output: A markdown rule file named hookify.console-log.local.md with frontmatter setting event to file and two conditions: file_path matching a TypeScript extension and new_text containing console.log. The message body explains why debug logs should not ship to production and suggests using a logging library.

output_examples.input: Write a rule that blocks rm -rf commands.
output_examples.output: A markdown rule file named hookify.dangerous-rm.local.md with frontmatter setting event to bash, action to block, and pattern to the regex for rm followed by the recursive-force flag. The message explains the command was blocked because it can delete files irreversibly and suggests safer alternatives.

best_practices: Use descriptive, action-oriented kebab-case rule names that start with a verb, such as warn-console-log or block-dangerous-rm.
Prefer unquoted YAML patterns so a single backslash works as written, and reserve the block action for genuinely dangerous operations.
Test each pattern against real and near-miss inputs before relying on it, since a too-broad pattern creates noise and a too-specific one misses matches.
anti_patterns: Writing overly broad patterns like the bare word log that match unrelated text such as login, dialog, and catalog.
Forgetting to escape regex metacharacters, so a dot or parenthesis matches far more than intended.
Blocking routine operations by default, which trains users to ignore warnings instead of reserving blocks for real risks.

faq.question: Where are hookify rules stored?
faq.answer: Rules live in the .claude directory and are named hookify.{descriptive-name}.local.md. Add .claude/*.local.md to your gitignore so local rules stay out of version control.

faq.question: What is the difference between the warn and block actions?
faq.answer: The warn action shows a message but allows the operation to continue and is the default. The block action prevents the operation or stops the session, so reserve it for genuinely dangerous actions.

faq.question: Which events can a rule trigger on?
faq.answer: A rule can trigger on bash commands, file edits, stop events, prompt submissions, or all events. You set this with the event field in the frontmatter.

faq.question: How do I write a rule that checks more than one condition?
faq.answer: Use the advanced conditions format. Each condition has a field, an operator such as regex_match or contains, and a pattern. All conditions must match for the rule to trigger.

faq.question: Do I need to restart anything after adding a rule?
faq.answer: No. Rules are read dynamically, so changes take effect on the next tool use. You can test a new or edited rule immediately.

faq.question: Does this skill run the dangerous commands it mentions?
faq.answer: No. The skill is documentation only. Commands and regex patterns like rm -rf or eval appear as examples of what a rule should detect and warn about, and the skill never executes them.
